1._section_summary: This abstract describes a single study (Study X) that investigated the indirect effects of overhearing family fat talk on mindful eating, mediated by body appreciation and functional body appreciation, among 333 undergraduate women from a southeastern public university. Participants completed an online survey. The study found an inverse association between family fat talk and mindful eating, body appreciation, and functional body appreciation, with functional body appreciation explaining the link between family fat talk and mindful eating, even after controlling for BMI.

2.evidence_source: In this context, the present study extends previous research grounded in the sociocultural model supporting the specific role of family influences (i.e., parental commentary) on negative body image and maladaptive eating processes in college women in two important ways (Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009b,). Therefore, the current analysis provides a preliminary evaluation of a partial sociocultural model of mindful eating informed by the Tripartite Influence framework (Rodgers et al., 2009b; Thompson et al., 1999) in a college female sample.
2._section_summary: This introduction section discusses the Tripartite Influence Model and the impact of family appearance-related commentary and fat talk on body image and eating behaviors, particularly in women. The present study aims to extend this research by evaluating a partial sociocultural model of mindful eating in a college female sample, focusing on family fat talk, body appreciation, functional body appreciation, and mindful eating as key variables.

16.extract_value: This section details the four stages of data analysis, including data inspection, descriptive statistics, basic correlations between key study variables, and the use of Hayes' (2013) PROCESS macro model 4 for SPSS to detect potential indirect effects using multiple regression of z-scores, adjusted for BMI. The robust analytic approach involved 10,000 random resamples with replacement.
16.evidence_source: The data analyses were carried out in four stages. First, we inspected the data to evaluate the amount of missingness at the variable level and determined whether a systematic pattern occurred. Second, basic descriptive statistics were conducted to assess whether the distributional characteristics of the data met assumptions of normality. Third, to address the first hypothesis, basic correlations were computed to establish the linear associations between the key study variables. Lastly, Hayes' (2013) PROCESS macro model 4 for SPSS was used to detect the potential predicted indirect effects using multiple regression of the zscores for each variable in a combined model adjusted for BMI. This non-parametric method is based on a bootstrap resampling technique and yields an indirect effect beta coefficient estimate alongside a biascorrected 95% confidence interval (CI). Statistical significance is demonstrated when the 95% CI excludes zero. Ten thousand random resamples with replacement were performed for the multiple indirect model. This robust analytic approach is now considered the strategy of choice over the traditional Baron and Kenny (1986) causal steps test of mediation and the corresponding Sobel test (Sobel, 1982) for more directly evaluating the magnitude and significance of an indirect effect (Preacher & Hayes, 2008).

21.extract_value: This discussion section presents the preliminary evaluation of a sociocultural model of mindful eating, focusing on the impact of overhearing family 'fat talk' on mindful eating through positive body image variables. The findings largely supported the hypotheses, showing an inverse association between family fat talk and mindful eating, general body appreciation, and body functionality. 21.evidence_source: The present study provided a preliminary evaluation of a sociocultural model of mindful eating grounded in the larger Tripartite Influence Model (Thompson et al., 1999) and supported by research illuminating the specific role of family factors (e.g., parental commentary) in this theoretical framework (e.g., Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009a; Rodgers et al., 2009b). Specifically, we assessed whether the frequency of overhearing family members complaining about their own physical appearance (i.e., fat talk) negatively predicted mindful eating through two closely-related positive body image variables. Results were mostly in the hypothesized directions. As predicted, overhearing family participate in self-denigrating body commentary was inversely associated with mindful eating, general body appreciation, and specifically appreciating the body's functionality. Additionally, more frequent mindful eating corresponded with higher levels of both positive body image indices. We also found partial support for our initial test of the sociocultural model in predicting mindful eating in the current sample. When considered in concert, only an appreciation for the body's functionality (or body-as-process; Franzoi, 1995) emerged as a significant (albeit modest in size) explanatory mechanism in the link between family fat talk disclosures and overall mindful eating behavior. Overall, our preliminary findings extend earlier tests of family-related influences such as direct parental commentary stemming from sociocultural theory (Thompson et al., 1999) in predicting negative body image and disordered eating (e.g., Kluck, 2010; Rodgers et al., 2009a; Rodgers et al., 2009b). We demonstrated that this model featuring the indirect influence of overhearing family fat talk can be successfully applied to accounting for variability in positive body image and mindful eating in a college female sample.

1._section_summary: This abstract describes a single study (Study X) that investigated the indirect effects of overhearing family fat talk on mindful eating, mediated by body appreciation and functional body appreciation, among 333 undergraduate women from a southeastern public university. Participants completed an online survey. The study found an inverse association between family fat talk and mindful eating, body appreciation, and functional body appreciation, with functional body appreciation explaining the link between family fat talk and mindful eating, even after controlling for BMI.

The model examined the unique effects of positive body image mediating variables on mindful eating scores, controlling for multicollinearity. Key findings included the full model accounting for 20% of the variance in mindful eating scores, with specific beta weights reported for BMI, FFTQ-F, BAS-2, and FBApS.
